transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Well, I suppose I'm here because... well, honestly, it's been an incredibly stressful few months. I’ve lived in my apartment for a good while, and as a management analyst, I’m trained to look for patterns, right? To see how systems operate, how variables interact. And what’s been happening is—well, it’s not a coincidence. For months now, the property manager, along with certain individuals in the building, have been running a very coordinated, very deliberate campaign to pressure me out of my unit. 

It started small, you know? Just... mail being misdelivered. Not just junk mail, but important documents, bank statements, things that shouldn't just "accidentally" end up in the wrong box week after week. I documented it, of course. Then it escalated to these timed noises in the walls. Thumping, scraping, always right when I’m trying to sleep or focus on my work. It’s not just settling pipes; it’s rhythmic, it’s intentional. And then there are the neighbors. People I used to just nod at in the hallway are suddenly making these little comments, dropping hints about how "some people" overstay their welcome, or how the building is "changing." 

I’ve brought this up to management, naturally. I’ve shown them the logs I’ve kept, the timelines of the noises, the missing mail reports. And they just smile and hand me all this paperwork, these supposed explanations about plumbing work or postal errors. But no amount of their paperwork or their polite little excuses changes the pattern I can see right in front of me. They want me out, and they’re using every subtle tactic they can to make it happen. It’s exhausting, frankly, having to constantly be on guard in your own home.
During this time, have you had a period where your mood felt unusually high, energized, or euphoric?

High? Euphoric? Well, no... no, certainly not. I'm not sure how anyone could possibly feel euphoric under these kinds of conditions, to be perfectly honest with you. 

I mean, if you really look at the day-to-day reality of what I'm dealing with, it’s just a constant, grinding pressure. You have to understand, when
Have you been hearing voices when no one is actually there?

Voices? No. No, certainly not. I mean, let's be perfectly clear here, Doctor, I am a management analyst. My entire career—nearly forty years of it, mind you, ever since I finished my graduate program—has been built entirely on observing tangible, verifiable data. I don't hear things that aren't there. If I hear a sound, it is because a sound has been produced in the physical environment. 

Now, do I hear the scraping? Yes. Do I hear the rhythmic thumping in the walls at 2:00 AM? Absolutely. But those are acoustic realities, deliberately generated by the people in my building who are trying to force me out of my lease. They are mechanical noises, structural noises. I've even tried to record them, though the frequencies are often just low enough to evade the standard microphone pickup on a smartphone, which, quite frankly, just points to a highly sophisticated and calculated effort on their part. 

But voices? Like whispers in an empty room or people talking in my head? Absolutely not. I am perfectly sound of mind, which is exactly why this whole situation is so incredibly frustrating to navigate. When you have a perfectly logical, grounded grasp on reality, and you can clearly see the variables interacting—the missing mail, the timed noises, the passive-aggressive comments from the neighbors—it is profoundly insulting when management tries to imply that it might just be some trick of the mind. So no, I assure you, there are no voices. Just the very real, very documented sounds of a harassment campaign that no one wants to take responsibility for.
Did these experiences begin after a medical illness, head injury, or new medication?

Medical illness? A head injury? No, no, certainly not. I understand why you’re asking, of course. As an analyst, I fully appreciate the need to rule out external variables—you have to go down your clinical checklist to make sure there isn't some biological factor skewing the data, so to speak. It's basic deductive reasoning. But I can assure you, my physical health is remarkably stable for a man of sixty-five. I haven't had any head trauma, no accidents, no hospitalizations, nothing of the sort. 

And as for medications, I don't even take any prescriptions. I take a standard daily multivitamin, and perhaps an occasional ibuprofen if I've spent too many consecutive hours reviewing documents and spreadsheets at my desk, but absolutely nothing new has been introduced into my system. 

So, no, there is absolutely no medical catalyst for what is happening to me. And frankly, Doctor, that is exactly what makes this whole situation so insidious. The property manager—and I’m quite sure they’ve consulted with their legal department on how to handle me—they would absolutely love it if I had suddenly started some mind-altering new medication or taken a hit to the head. It would be the perfect excuse for them, wouldn't it? They could just wave away all my meticulous logs, the timelines, the missing mail reports, and paint it all as the confused ramblings of an older tenant with a medical issue. 

But my cognitive faculties are just as sharp as they were when I finished my graduate program. If anything, my absolute clarity of mind is exactly what has allowed me to uncover their campaign in the first place. If I were actually impaired by a medication or an injury, I might have just ignored the missing bank statements, or I might have just assumed the 2:00 AM scraping noises were normal building settling. But I didn't. I saw the pattern because my brain is functioning perfectly. So no, no injuries, no illnesses, no new pills whatsoever. Just the verifiable facts of what they are doing to me.
About how long have these problems with the neighbors and property manager been going on?

Well, let me think... if we look at the timeline objectively, I would say this has been going on for about eleven months now. Yes, eleven months. It all started shortly after I moved into this new apartment. 

I remember the exact timeframe because I signed the lease in the early spring, and I had spent a considerable amount of time reviewing the property, looking at the layout, analyzing the commute—you know, doing my due diligence, as I do with any major decision. The first few weeks were relatively quiet, which, in hindsight, was clearly just a baseline period. They were letting me get settled, letting me unpack, letting me establish a routine so they could figure out exactly how to disrupt it. 

It wasn't until about month two—so, roughly eleven months ago from today—that the first incident occurred. It started small, of course. A piece of mail delayed here, a strange look from a neighbor there. At first, I thought, 'Well, perhaps it's just the adjustment period of a new building.' But as an analyst, you learn that isolated incidents are rarely just isolated incidents when they start clustering together. By the third month, the scraping noises started. By the fourth, the passive-aggressive behavior in the hallways became undeniable. 

So, yes, eleven months. Eleven months of this calculated, relentless pressure. And they know exactly what they're doing, Doctor. They stretch it out over a long period—eleven months is a very specific duration for this kind of psychological attrition—because they think if they do it slowly enough, I'll either break down or just leave voluntarily without them having to go through the formal, legal eviction process. It’s a classic strategy, really. But I’ve been documenting every single day of those eleven months, so I have the entire trajectory mapped out.
Have you noticed yourself becoming much less interested in socializing or doing the things you usually enjoy?

Less interested in socializing? No, no, I wouldn't say that at all. In fact, it's quite the opposite in terms of my capacity for engagement, although the circumstances have certainly shifted the *nature* of my interactions. Let me explain, because it's a very important distinction to make when you're looking at behavioral data. 

I am still very much the same person I was before I signed that lease. I still enjoy a good intellectual debate, I still appreciate a well-structured analysis of current events, and I still have a deep appreciation for the hobbies I've cultivated over my lifetime. I haven't lost interest in the world, Doctor. Not by a long shot. 

However, when you are the target of a coordinated campaign designed specifically to destabilize your living situation, your priorities naturally have to adapt. It’s a simple matter of resource allocation. If I used to spend, say, three evenings a week attending lectures or meeting with former colleagues for dinner—which I very much enjoyed, mind you—I now have to weigh the cost-benefit of leaving my apartment unattended. Can I really afford to go out and socialize when I know, based on eleven months of empirical evidence, that the moment I leave, they might slip into my unit to tamper with my files? Or that they might use my absence to escalate the noise campaign, perhaps testing new frequencies while I'm not there to document them? 

So, it's not a lack of interest, you see. It's a strategic withdrawal. I am simply prioritizing the defense of my space and the documentation of their activities over casual socialization. It requires an immense amount of focus. I have to stay vigilant. I have to monitor the hallway traffic, log the times the scraping noises occur, and cross-reference the missing mail with the shifts of the property management staff. It’s practically a full-time job on top of my actual consulting work. 

And frankly, it’s difficult to enjoy a casual conversation with an old friend when you know what’s waiting for you back home. How can I sit there and discuss golf or the stock market when I know there's a highly sophisticated effort underway to force me out of my home? The disparity between their mundane concerns and the very real, very pressing reality of my situation is just... it's vast. So, no, I haven't lost interest in life. I am just intensely focused on managing a very complex, very hostile set of variables that demand my full attention.
Have other people told you that you seem less emotionally expressive than you used to?

Less emotionally expressive? No, no, I can't say anyone has brought that up. I haven't had anyone tell me I seem... what, blank? Unfeeling? No, certainly not. 

I suppose I can see why you might ask that. You’re looking for signs that I’m shutting down, perhaps? But no, quite the opposite, really. If I'm speaking with my brother on the phone, for instance—though we do speak a bit less often now, given my need to monitor the premises—I am just as engaged, just as articulate about my feelings and frustrations as I ever was. My emotional range is perfectly intact. 

If anything, Doctor, the sheer audacity of what this property management company is doing has elicited a very strong, very appropriate emotional response from me. Indignation. A highly focused, righteous indignation. When I confronted the superintendent last month about the fresh scratch marks I found around my deadbolt, I assure you, I was incredibly expressive. I laid out the facts, I presented my timeline, and my tone conveyed exactly how unacceptable the situation was. There was nothing lacking in my emotional delivery, I promise you that. 

I think sometimes people confuse a disciplined, analytical demeanor with a lack of emotion. As an analyst, I've always had to maintain a certain professional composure. You have to do that when you're presenting complex data sets to a board of directors. You simply cannot let your personal feelings cloud the metrics. But that is self-regulation, you see. That is control. It is entirely different from a lack of expression. 

So, if, say, one of the neighbors—one of the ones who is clearly participating in this harassment—were to claim I seem "cold" or "unexpressive" when I pass them in the hallway, well, that’s simply because I am refusing to engage in their theatrical little games. I give them absolutely nothing to work with. I give them a blank wall. But that is a conscious, tactical choice on my part to deny them the satisfaction of seeing me rattled. It is not some sort of psychological fading away. So, to answer your question directly, no, no one of any consequence has suggested I’ve lost my emotional expressiveness. I am simply reserving it for when it actually matters.
Have you felt that anyone can control your thoughts or put thoughts into your mind?

Control my thoughts? Put thoughts into my mind? No, no, absolutely not. Let's be very, very clear about that, Doctor, because I think it's crucial you understand the distinction between external harassment and internal cognitive integrity. 

My mind is entirely my own. In fact, my analytical capacity is my greatest asset in this entire situation. It is the one thing they absolutely cannot compromise, no matter how hard they try. What they are doing—the property manager, the neighbors, the superintendent—it is all based on environmental manipulation. They operate in the physical space. They delay the mail, they create the scraping noises, they engage in the hallway theater... all of which is designed to apply psychological pressure from the *outside*. But they do not have access to my internal thoughts. 

Frankly, the idea of someone putting thoughts into my head is... well, it’s science fiction. I am a management analyst. I have a graduate degree. My entire career has been built on my ability to independently synthesize data, evaluate variables, and draw my own objective conclusions. When I document an incident, or when I deduce their underlying strategy, those are my thoughts. They are the result of my own rigorous, empirical observation. Nobody is beaming ideas into my skull. If I conclude that the property manager is trying to circumvent eviction laws, that isn't a thought someone "put" there. That is a logical deduction derived from observing their behavior over the last eleven months. 

If anything, Doctor, they are terrified of my thoughts. They are deeply threatened by my ability to think critically about what they are doing. They want to distract me, certainly. They want to exhaust me so that I stop thinking so clearly, so that I stop connecting the dots and documenting the timeline. That’s the whole point of the constant vigilance I have to maintain. But control my mind? Insert thoughts? No. No, I am the sole author of my own thoughts, and my cognitive faculties are as sharp as they have ever been. That is exactly why their little campaign hasn't succeeded in driving me out. I can see exactly what they're doing because my mind is completely, entirely under my own control.
During these past eleven months, have you had a period of at least two weeks when you felt depressed most of the day nearly every day?

Depressed? No, no. Let's be very precise about our terms here, Doctor, because I think it’s incredibly important that we don't conflate a highly rational response to an external threat with some sort of internal, pathological mood disorder. 

Depression implies a sort of... well, a collapse, doesn't it? A giving up. A pervasive sadness or lethargy that just arises from within, where you lose the will to get out of bed or fight for yourself. I have not experienced anything even remotely resembling that. Not for two weeks, not for two days. 

Have I been frustrated? Absolutely. Have I been exhausted by the sheer logistical weight of what I am dealing with? Without question. When you are forced to maintain a constant, unyielding state of vigilance—when you are meticulously logging every scrape against your floorboards, every missing piece of mail, like that certified letter from my accountant that conveniently vanished back in April, which I am still actively investigating, by the way—it takes a physical toll. It takes a toll on your stamina. But that is fatigue, Doctor. That is justifiable, situational fatigue, coupled with a very healthy dose of righteous anger. It is not depression. 

I really need to make sure you understand this distinction, because if you were to write "depressed" in my chart, it would completely misrepresent the empirical reality of my situation. Frankly, the property management company would absolutely love it if I were depressed. If I were depressed, I’d pull the covers over my head. I’d stop checking the hallway monitors. I’d stop documenting the superintendent's erratic shift changes. I would just surrender. 

But I am up every single morning at 5:30 AM. I am at my desk, I am reviewing my logs, I am cross-referencing the noise anomalies with the HVAC maintenance schedules. A depressed person simply does not have the drive, the cognitive stamina, or the sheer willpower to compile a comprehensive, evidence-based dossier on property management malfeasance. They just don't. So, to answer your question, no. I have not felt depressed. I am highly motivated, I am deeply engaged in defending my livelihood, and I am entirely focused on holding these people accountable.
Has anyone told you that your speech or behavior has seemed disorganized or hard to follow?

Disorganized? Hard to follow? No, no, I... quite the opposite, actually. 

I mean, you have to consider my background, Doctor. I am a management analyst. You simply do not survive in my field—let alone thrive in it—if you cannot present a coherent, linear, and highly structured narrative. My entire career has been predicated on taking chaotic, disorganized data from various departments and synthesizing it into extremely precise, easy-to-follow executive summaries. So, no, my speech is certainly not hard to follow. 

If anything, I am perhaps overly meticulous in how I articulate myself. For example, when I went down to the leasing office the other day regarding the... the sudden, unexplained power fluctuations in my unit—fluctuations that, interestingly enough, only seem to occur when I am compiling my daily logs—I didn't just walk in there and start rambling. I didn't lose my train of thought. I presented the property manager with a printed, itemized list. I had the dates, I had the timestamps, I had the exact duration of each outage. I laid it out point by point. A, B, C. It was an airtight presentation. 

Now, did he *feign* confusion? Did he try to play dumb? Of course he did. That’s standard evasion. He said something along the lines of, "I'm not following you, I don't know what you're getting at." But he
Have you ever felt that something external was making your body move or act against your own will?

Move or act against my will? Like a puppet on a string? No. No, absolutely not. That is... that is entirely outside the realm of what is happening here, Doctor. 

Just like I said about my thoughts, my body is completely my own. I control my own actions, entirely. Every step I take, every time I pick up my pen to document a new incident, every time I check the peephole because I hear them pacing out there—that is all me. I am making a conscious, deliberate choice to act. 

The idea of some sort of external force physically manipulating my limbs or forcing me to walk or speak... well, that’s just absurd. It’s physically impossible. What they are doing is psychological warfare, Doctor. It’s environmental manipulation. They are trying to force my hand, yes, in the sense that they want me to break my lease and move out. They want to create conditions that are so intolerable that I *choose* to leave. But they cannot physically make my legs walk out the door. They cannot physically make my hand sign a termination agreement. 

If they had that kind of power, if they could just take over my motor functions, they wouldn't need to bother with the scraping noises, would they? They wouldn't need to intercept my mail or mess with the HVAC system. They could just march me right down to the leasing office and make me hand over my keys. But they can't. Because they don't have that power. I am in complete control of my physical self. My autonomy is intact. 

In fact, my physical discipline is one of the things that keeps me grounded. I maintain a very strict routine. I stretch every morning, I make my coffee, I sit at my desk, I review my logs. I am very deliberate in my movements. I don't pace aimlessly. I don't fidget. When I move, I move with purpose. When I went down to the leasing office to confront them about the power fluctuations, I walked in there with perfect posture, completely composed. I didn't stumble, I wasn't shaking. I was in absolute control. So no, nothing is making my body move against my will. I am the sole master of my own physical actions, just as I am the master of my own mind.
During this time, have these beliefs about your neighbors and property manager been present continuously for at least one full month?

A month? Oh, Doctor, if it had only been a month, I might have just written it off as a string of unfortunate coincidences or perhaps a temporary adjustment period. But no, no, we are far, far past the one-month mark. This has been a continuous, unrelenting campaign for about eleven months now. 

It started almost immediately after I moved in. I signed the lease, I got my keys, I moved my furniture in—which, by the way, I supervised personally, ensuring every piece was placed exactly according to the floor plan I had drawn up—and within... I'd say within the first two weeks, the anomalies began. At first, it was subtle. A scrape here, a thump there. The sort of thing you might initially dismiss as normal building settling. But as a management analyst, I am trained to look for patterns in data, Doctor. And the pattern emerged very quickly. 

By the end of that first month, it was glaringly obvious that this was not random. And it has not stopped since. Every single day for eleven months, I have had to document these incidents. I have filled three—no, wait, I'm halfway through my fourth—four ledger books with meticulous, timestamped entries. If you were to look at my logs from, say, October, and compare them to my logs from just last Tuesday, you would see a clear, unbroken continuum of harassment. 

So, yes, a month is a vast understatement. It has been nearly a year of continuous, daily vigilance on my part. Eleven months of documenting, analyzing, and defending myself against this coordinated effort to force me out of my home. And I assure you, Doctor, I have no intention of letting up, no matter how long they decide to drag this out.
Have you ever seen things that other people could not see?

See things? You mean... like hallucinations? Phantoms? No. No, absolutely not. I understand exactly what you are getting at with that question, Doctor, and let me be perfectly clear: my visual acuity is entirely intact, and my perception of reality is firmly grounded in empirical evidence. I do not see ghosts, I do not see floating lights, I do not see anything that isn't physically, tangibly present in the room with me. 

Now, do I notice things that other people miss? Yes, certainly. But that is a matter of superior observation, not hallucination. For instance, when I look at the weather stripping around my front door, I can see the minute, millimeter-deep scratches where someone has clearly been trying to slide a tool in to bypass the deadbolt. If I were to point that out to the maintenance man—which I have, on several occasions—he might claim he doesn't see it, or he might try to brush it off and say it's just normal wear and tear. But that is not because the scratches aren't there. It is because he is either willfully ignoring them as part of their plausible deniability strategy, or he simply lacks the analytical training to recognize what he is looking at. 

My entire career... well, forty years in the field, I am sixty-five now, but my entire professional life has been built on seeing the details that others overlook. The discrepancies in a quarterly financial report, the hidden inefficiencies in a corporate supply chain, the subtle signs of tampering on a residential lock. These are real, physical phenomena. If I see something, it is because it exists in the physical world. 

I don't deal in illusions, Doctor. I deal in hard, actionable data. So if you are asking if my mind is conjuring up images out of thin air, the answer is an unequivocal no. Everything I see, everything I document in my ledgers, is objectively verifiable, provided the person verifying it is actually willing to open their eyes and look honestly at the evidence I am presenting to them.
Since this started, has your ability to work and manage your day-to-day life gotten worse?

Gotten worse? Well, that depends entirely on how you define "worse," Doctor. If you mean, am I failing to manage my life? Am I sitting around in a state of helpless confusion? Absolutely not. I am managing a highly complex, adversarial situation with extreme precision. 

But, if you are asking if my daily schedule has been disrupted... well, yes, inevitably. You have to understand, when you are subjected to a constant, coordinated campaign of environmental manipulation, you have to reallocate your resources. It’s basic crisis management. You triage. 

Because of this, I've actually had to... well, I’ve pulled back from several of my consulting jobs recently. I usually keep three or four active clients—efficiency audits, organizational restructuring, that sort of thing—but I simply cannot dedicate the requisite forty hours a week to analyzing their corporate supply chains when my own immediate environment requires such intense, daily surveillance. It wouldn't be fair to my clients, and it would leave me vulnerable here. 

So, instead of settling into my normal work, I find myself spending a vast majority of my week—we're talking Monday through Friday, easily—managing this situation. I am constantly following up with the leasing office, cornering the building staff to demand answers about the maintenance logs, and attempting to speak with the neighbors on my floor to determine who is actively complicit and who is just turning a blind eye. It is practically a full-time job in itself just holding them accountable. 

And my painting... I don't know if I mentioned this to you, but I have been an avid painter for over twenty years. Oils, mostly. Architectural studies and landscapes. It requires a tremendous amount of focus, a certain... tranquility. You have to be able to settle into the canvas. But how can I settle into my normal painting routine when I have to keep one ear trained on the hallway at all times? I can't. If I start mixing my paints and they begin that rhythmic scraping on the floorboards above me, the paint just dries on the palette while I have to go log the incident and check the perimeter. 

So, my easel just sits there in the corner, covered with a drop cloth. I haven't finished a piece in months. My day-to-day life hasn't "gotten worse" in the sense of a decline in my abilities, Doctor. My abilities are sharper than ever. It is simply that my time and energy have been completely hijacked by the sheer necessity of defending my own territory.
Have you ever had the experience that an ordinary event or object suddenly took on a special meaning meant specifically for you?

Special meaning... well, if you phrase it like that, it sounds like some sort of mystical revelation, which, as I have just explained, is entirely outside my purview. I don't do mysticism, Doctor. I deal in empirical facts. But if you are asking whether I look at an ostensibly "ordinary" event and recognize that it is, in fact, a targeted variable in a larger equation meant specifically for me... then yes. Absolutely. That is precisely why I am sitting in this chair talking to you today. 

Because for months now, I have been tracking these so-called "ordinary" events, and they are anything but ordinary. Take the mail, for example. To a layman, a misdelivered piece of mail is just a bureaucratic hiccup. A mistake by the post office. But when you track the frequency, when you see that my important financial documents are consistently being diverted, or that my neighbors' junk mail is being shoved into my box with aggressive force on specific days of the week... you realize it’s not an accident. It is a calculated tactic. 

Or the sounds in the building. A thump in the wall is ordinary, right? Just pipes settling, they say. But these are timed noises in the walls. If I walk from the kitchen to the living room, the tapping follows the exact trajectory of my footsteps. If I sit down to read, a low, rhythmic thudding starts directly behind my headboard. That is not plumbing, Doctor. That is intentional harassment. 

And then there are the people in the building. Certain neighbors who are clearly in on it. You pass them in the lobby and they make these little comments. "Sure is getting crowded around here," or "Hope you're packing light these days." Just little, insidious jabs, delivered with perfect plausible deniability. Anyone else might brush it off as small talk, but I know exactly what it means. 

The property manager and certain people in the building have been using these exact tactics
Have you believed that the people in your building are using any impossible technology or supernatural means to monitor or influence you?

Impossible technology? Supernatural means? Doctor, I... frankly, I find the phrasing of that question a little insulting, given everything I’ve just explained to you about my methodology and my reliance on empirical evidence. I am a management analyst, not a science fiction writer. I thought we had firmly established my stance on mysticism and fantasy just a moment ago. 

I don't believe in ghosts, I don't believe in telepathy, and I certainly don't believe anyone is using "impossible" technology against me. Why on earth would they need to? The technology required to monitor a person in a modern apartment building is entirely possible, entirely mundane, and frankly, it is readily available to anyone with a basic internet connection and a credit card. 

You don't need a magic wand or some top-secret government satellite beam to track my movements. You just need a cheap acoustic listening device pressed against the drywall. You can buy them online for fifty dollars. Plumbers use them to find leaks behind walls, but a malicious neighbor or a complicit maintenance worker can just as easily use one to hear exactly where I am walking in my apartment, which explains how they track my footsteps so precisely. That isn't supernatural, Doctor. That's just basic acoustics. 

And as for influencing me... there is no mind control happening here. Nobody is beaming thoughts into my head. What they are doing is engaging in psychological attrition. It’s the constant, low-grade stress of knowing your mail is being handled, of hearing those deliberate, timed thuds on the ceiling the second you try to read, of finding those micro-scratches on the door frame. It is a very terrestrial, very human campaign of harassment. 

The property manager doesn't need impossible technology when he already has the master keys to the building, access to the utility closets, and a staff that is clearly willing to do his dirty work. It’s all very physical. It’s all very real. So, no. No supernatural means whatsoever. Just standard, highly coordinated, thoroughly documented harassment using everyday tools. As I said, I deal in facts, and the facts of this situation are firmly, undeniably rooted in the physical world.
Has anyone ever told you that your beliefs about the property manager and neighbors seem implausible or impossible, rather than just unlikely?

Implausible? Impossible? Oh, constantly. Constantly, Doctor. That is the... well, it’s the standard defense mechanism, isn't it? When you present someone with a complex, uncomfortable reality that they simply don't want to deal with, their first instinct is to just wave their hands and dismiss it as "impossible." 

I have sat down with the regional director of the management company, for instance. I requested a formal meeting, brought my binders, my incident logs, everything perfectly indexed and cross-referenced. And he had the absolute audacity to sit there behind his mahogany desk, look at my documentation, and tell me that what I was suggesting was logistically impossible. He actually used that exact word. "Impossible." He told me I was leaping to wildly implausible conclusions over ordinary apartment living.

But you see, Doctor, I am here—sitting in this very office, taking time out of my day to speak with you—because for months now, the property manager and certain people in the building have been using these exact tactics. The purposefully misdelivered mail, the timed noises in the walls that track my movements, those insidious little comments from the neighbors in the lobby... it is all part of a highly coordinated effort to pressure me out of the apartment. It is a textbook constructive eviction campaign, designed to look like a series of unrelated accidents to the untrained eye. 

And they try to cover it up, of course. They try to make me look like the one who is jumping at shadows. The property manager will pull out these fabricated maintenance logs to prove no one was working on the pipes, or the post office will send me some boilerplate form letter about "sorting errors at the regional hub," trying to explain away the anomalies. They throw all this bureaucratic chaff in the air to obscure the truth. 

But I am an analyst. I analyze complex systems for a living. I know how to separate noise from data. And I can tell you, with absolute, unshakeable certainty, that no amount of their paperwork or explanations changes the pattern I can see. They can call it impossible all they want. They can try to gaslight me with forged work orders and fake smiles. But the pattern is there, the intent is clear, and I absolutely refuse to let them convince me that what I am experiencing with my own two eyes and ears is somehow impossible.
Have you ever felt that other people could hear or know your thoughts as you were thinking them?

Hear my thoughts? Doctor, please. I... I really must ask where you are pulling these questions from, because it feels as though you are entirely ignoring the foundation of everything I have just laid out for you. Hear my thoughts? No. Absolutely not. That is... well, it’s just biological nonsense, isn't it? 

Thoughts are internal cognitive processes. They are closed-loop electrical impulses firing inside the brain. Unless someone has physically breached my skull and implanted some sort of experimental neural interface—which, for the record, they have not, as I have no surgical scars and, again, I do not subscribe to science fiction—there is absolutely no physical mechanism by which another human being could "hear" what I am thinking. 

If they could read my mind, Doctor, why on earth would they bother with the acoustic listening devices? Why would they need to track my footsteps through the floorboards or monitor my mail to see my financial statements? The very fact that they are expending so much effort on physical surveillance—the mail tampering, the timed thuds, the coordinated harassment in the lobby—proves objectively that they do not have access to my internal monologue. They have to rely on external data gathering, just like any other terrestrial intelligence operation.
